entries.title: Cosmic microwave background
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a cosmic-microwave-background page. Fixsen 2009 gives T0 = 2.72548 ± 0.00057 K. The calculator uses the central value and CODATA 2018’s exact h, c, and k. The wavelength peak, b/T with b from the root of (5−x)e^x = 5, is 1.0632 mm. The frequency peak, from the root of (3−x)e^x = 3, is 160.229 GHz, which is 58.789 GHz per kelvin. c/λ_max is 281.968 GHz and is not that peak. The photon density 16π ζ(3) (kT/hc)^3 is 410.7 per cm³. The radiation constant a = 4σ/c prints as 7.5657 × 10^−16 J m^−3 K^−4, and aT^4 is 4.1747 × 10^−14 J/m³. Ideal blackbody scaling is T(z) = T0(1+z). z = 1 is 5.45096 K. z = 6 is 19.07836 K. Planck 2018 results VI, Table 2, z* = 1089.92 ± 0.25, gives 2973.28 K and a wavelength peak of 974.6 nm, infrared, next to the 700 nm visible edge. Planck 2018 results I, Table 2, lists the dipole amplitude 3362.08 ± 0.99 µK. ΔT = T0 v/c turns that into 369.82 km/s, and ΔT/T is 1.2336 × 10^−3. The smaller anisotropies are about 1 part in 10^5. The disk is a schematic, not a sky map. Not a power spectrum.

entries.title: Sundial and shadow length
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a sundial page. Solar altitude and azimuth follow NOAA’s solar calculator, the Meeus series on the Global Monitoring Laboratory calculation-details page. Longitude is positive east. Atmospheric refraction is not applied. Shadow length of a vertical object is its height divided by the tangent of the altitude. Below the horizon, and within 0.2° of it, the page reports no useful finite shadow. At Campbell, 37.287° N and 121.950° W, on 21 June 2026 with the clock at UTC−7, solar noon is 13:10, declination is 23.437°, altitude is 76.15°, and a 1.8 m person casts 0.44 m. The classroom estimate 90 − 37.29 + 23.44 is 76.15°, and 1.8 divided by the tangent of that angle is 0.44 m. On 21 December 2026, UTC−8, solar noon is 12:06, declination is −23.438°, altitude is 29.28°, and the shadow is 3.21 m. The matching estimate is 29.27° and 3.21 m. From 2020 through 2030 the equation of time in this series stays between −14.24 and +16.49 minutes. A horizontal dial’s hour lines use tan θ = sin φ · tan(15° × (t − 12)), the relation Carl Sabanski prints, with the style angle equal to the latitude. The day’s curve is the shadow of a nodus on that style. At the equator those hour lines coincide. The Tropic of Cancer button is 23.44° N, the Earth Fact Sheet obliquity, and the noon shadow there can vanish. The Arctic Circle button is 66.56° N. Eratosthenes is told from NASA’s Imagine the Universe — 7.2°, 5,000 stadia, 250,000 stadia — and the Ohio State lecture that the stadion’s length is contentious: 185 m gives 46,250 km, while other values land nearer a modern 40,070 km. This page does not choose a stadion. Not for navigation or survey.

entries.title: Star trails and sky rotation
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a star-trails page. A fixed camera records Earth’s turn as an arc around the celestial pole. This page uses a mean sidereal day of 86,164.0905 s, the same rounding as the Foucault desk. JPL’s astrodynamic parameters print 86,164.09054 s. Rounded to four decimals in the seconds, that is 86,164.0905. The calculator uses 86,164.0905. A full circle divided by that day is 15.041069″ per second of time. The angle around the pole is that rate times the exposure. It does not depend on declination. The path on the sky is the same rate times cos δ. Thirty seconds at declination 0° is 7.52′ (451.23″). A 24 mm lens and an illustrative 5.9 µm pixel then drift 0.2966 px/s, which is 8.8989 px in those thirty seconds. One pixel of blur takes 3.371 s. The 500 rule, 500 / (crop factor × focal length), is 20.83 s at 24 mm and crop 1, and that allows 6.1798 px at this pitch and at the equator. Frédéric Michaud’s NPF rule, Société Astronomique du Havre, is used as printed: simplified (35 N + 30 p) / f is 11.46 s, and complete k (16.9 N + 0.10 f + 13.7 p) / (f cos δ) at k = 1 and f/2.8 is 5.440 s. The coefficients are not re-derived. At 60° the path and the drift are half, and the angle around the pole is unchanged. On the pole the path is zero. A perfect sidereal mount sets the sensor drift to zero and leaves periodic error out. From Campbell, 37.29° N, the pole’s altitude is 37.29°. The page opens on 30 minutes, which is 7.521°. Thirty minutes is 451.23′ because an arcminute is sixty arcseconds and thirty minutes is sixty times thirty seconds. Not an exposure to trust on a given night.

entries.title: Proper motion and space velocity
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a proper-motion page. Tangential speed is proper motion in arcseconds per year times distance in parsecs times one astronomical unit per Julian year. The IAU astronomical unit is 149,597,870.7 km. A Julian year is 365.25 × 86,400 s. The quotient is 4.74047046 km/s. Five-decimal rounding is 4.74047. The calculator uses the quotient. 4.74 is not substituted. Total proper motion is the root sum square of μ_α* and μ_δ. μ_α* is already multiplied by cos δ. Barnard's Star is Gaia DR3 4472832130942575872: parallax 546.9759 mas, μ_α* −801.551 mas/yr, μ_δ 10362.394 mas/yr, radial velocity −110.468 km/s. The total is 10.393349″/yr. The distance is 1.828234 pc. The tangential speed is 90.076 km/s. With the radial velocity the space velocity is 142.537 km/s, 140.81° from the outward line of sight. Half a degree, taken as a full-Moon width, is 1,800″, which takes 173.2 yr. One degree takes 346.4 yr. The straight-line closest approach is 9,719.8 yr from now, at 1.155347 pc. That is a linear approximation. The Sun is held fixed. Galactic acceleration is left out. Kapteyn's Star is receding at 245.053 km/s, so its straight-line minimum is in the past. Deneb uses the van Leeuwen 2007 parallax 2.31 mas and proper motion, and the Gontcharov 2006 radial velocity −4.9 km/s. Its tangential speed is 5.606 km/s. Formal errors are not folded in. Not an orbit.

entries.title: Atmospheric refraction
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an atmospheric-refraction page. Bennett 1982 from apparent altitude is R = cot(h_a + 7.31/(h_a + 4.4)) arcminutes. Sæmundsson 1986 from true altitude is R = 1.02 cot(h + 10.3/(h + 5.11)) arcminutes. Meeus multiplies both by (P/1010)×(283/(273+T)). At 0°, 1010 hPa, and 10°C, Bennett is 34.5′. The true altitude is −0.575°. Sæmundsson there is 34.4′. The gap is 0.037′. Sæmundsson at true altitude 0° is 29.0′. At 45° Bennett is 0.995′. At 90° the formula’s residual is −0.001′. It is not forced to zero. NOAA’s sunrise altitude is −0.833°, about 34′ plus about 16′ of semi-diameter. Bennett plus that 16′ puts the Sun’s center at −0.841°, geometrically below the horizon when the upper limb is on the apparent horizon. The horizontal diameter on this page is 32′, twice the 16′ allowance. The apparent vertical diameter, true diameter held at 32′ and the lower limb at apparent 0°, is 26.8′. The flattening is 5.18′. Extra daylight is the hour-angle difference: day length is 2H/15 hours, cos H = (sin a − sin φ sin δ)/(cos φ cos δ), between the center at −(R+16′) and at −16′. At Campbell, 37.29° N, and declination 0°, that is 5.78 min for sunrise and sunset together. The simple estimate 2R/(15°/h · cos φ · cos δ) is also 5.78 min because sin H is 1 at the equinox. NOAA’s fixed pair, −0.833° against −0.267°, is 5.69 min. At declination 23.44° the hour-angle extra is 6.71 min and the simple estimate is 6.30 min. Cold arctic air, −30°C and 1030 hPa, is 40.9′ at the horizon. Mauna Kea, 615 hPa and 0°C, is 21.8′. Meeus reports Bennett within 0.07′ of Garfinkel from the zenith to the horizon, and Sæmundsson within about 0.1′ of Bennett, for a standard atmosphere. Real horizon refraction varies with temperature inversions. The green flash and the Novaya Zemlya effect are named and not computed. Not a forecast.

entries.title: Foucault pendulum
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a Foucault page. The swing plane turns at Earth’s sidereal rotation times sin φ. This page uses a mean sidereal day of 86,164.0905 s, which is 23 h 56 m 4.0905 s, or 23.934470 mean solar hours. JPL’s astrodynamic parameters print 86,164.09054 s, cited to Seidelmann’s 1992 explanatory supplement. Rounded to four decimals in the seconds, that is 86,164.0905. The calculator uses 86,164.0905. The Earth Fact Sheet lists the sidereal rotation period as 23.9345 hours. 23.934470 rounds to 23.9345 at four decimals. Neither printed rounding is substituted. At 90° the period is one sidereal day, 23.934470 h, clockwise viewed from above. At 30° it is twice that, 47.868939 h. At the equator the plane does not precess. South of the equator the sign flips: Sydney at −33.87° is 42.946387 h, counter-clockwise viewed from above. Campbell, the local-sky desk’s 37.29° N, is 39.505632 h (39 h 30 m 20.2754 s), 9.08774° per sidereal hour. The Panthéon button, 48.85° N, is 31.785930 h (31 h 47 m 9.3482 s), 11.29484° per sidereal hour. Léon Foucault described the experiment in 1851, showed it at the Paris Observatory in February, and hung a long pendulum in the Panthéon in March. At the pole the plane stays fixed against the stars and the floor turns under it. Elsewhere only the part of the rotation along the local vertical, Ω sin φ, shows up. In the rotating frame that rate is Coriolis. A real pendulum needs a long wire, a heavy bob, and a drive or a Charron ring. This page leaves those out. Educational idealized model, not an engineering design.

entries.title: Aberration of starlight
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an aberration page. Earth moves, so a star’s apparent direction tilts toward that velocity. The Earth Fact Sheet prints a mean orbital velocity of 29.78 km/s. c is 299,792.458 km/s exactly. Their quotient at a right angle is 20.48939″. USNO Circular 163 prints the IAU (1976) constant of aberration for epoch 2000 as 20.49552″. 20.48939 is not substituted for 20.49552, and 20.49552 is not substituted for 20.48939. The difference at that speed between the first-order shift and the relativistic shift is 3.371 × 10^−8″. Vis-viva at the fact sheet’s perihelion, 147.095 × 10^6 km, is 30.287 km/s, and at aphelion, 152.100 × 10^6 km, is 29.291 km/s. Those round to the sheet’s 30.29 and 29.29. The sheet’s rounded speeds are not substituted. The equatorial speed is 2πR/T with R = 6,378.137 km and T = 23.9345 hours, which is 0.465101 km/s. At a right angle the diurnal angle is 0.32000″. 0.465101 rounds to 0.465 at three decimals. 0.465 is not substituted. NASA Science, for 21 August 2024, prints Voyager 1 at 17.0 km/s relative to the Sun. At 0.9c and θ = 90° the first-order angle is 51.56620°, the classical tan formula is 41.98721°, and the relativistic formula cos θ′ = (cos θ + β)/(1 + β cos θ) is 64.15807°. They are not averaged. James Bradley’s account was published in Philosophical Transactions 35, 637–661 (1729), after observations of γ Draconis meant to measure its parallax. van Leeuwen 2007 gives that star’s parallax as 21.14 ± 0.10 mas. 21.14 mas is 0.02114″. 1000/21.14 is 47.3037 pc. κ / 0.02114″ is 969.514. The year’s path is a circle of radius κ at the ecliptic pole, an ellipse with semi-minor axis κ |sin β|, and a line on the ecliptic. Parallax points toward the Sun. Aberration points along Earth’s velocity. They are a quarter-year apart. The ±0.10 mas is not folded in. Not an astrometric reduction.

entries.title: Supernova decay desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a supernova page. The late light is the chain 56Ni → 56Co → 56Fe. Nadyozhin 1994, ApJS 92, 527, prints half-lives 6.10 d and 77.12 d, mean lives 8.80 d and 111.3 d, and deposited energies 1.75 MeV per nickel decay and 3.73 MeV per cobalt decay. The 3.73 is 3.61 MeV of gamma rays plus 0.12 MeV of positron kinetic energy. Neutrinos, 0.41 MeV and 0.84 MeV, are left out. 6.10 / ln 2 rounds to 8.80. 77.12 / ln 2 is 111.26, which he rounds to 111.3. The calculator uses 8.80 and 111.3 because those are the lifetimes in his energy formula. One nucleus is 56 u. u is the 2022 CODATA value 1.66053906892×10^−27 kg. One MeV is 10^6 times the exact elementary charge, in joules. A solar mass is the IAU 2015 nominal GM☉, 1.3271244×10^20, divided by the 2022 CODATA G, 6.67430×10^−11, which is 1.9884098707×10^30 kg. The count per solar mass is 2.13830×10^55. The Bateman solution recomputes his combined coefficients as 6.44240×10^43 and 1.44295×10^43 erg/s per solar mass. He prints 6.45×10^43 and 1.45×10^43. They are not averaged. The curves use the Bateman solution. Full gamma-ray trapping: gamma rays and positron kinetic energy are deposited. Diffusion is not computed, so the curve falls from day 0. The cobalt count peaks at 24.2469 days, which rounds to the 24.25 days he prints. That day is not the optical peak. At 0.6 solar masses and day 24.25 the total is 9.41979×10^42 erg/s. Nickel is 3.00742×10^42. Cobalt is 6.41237×10^42. Nickel over cobalt is 0.4690. The shares are 31.93% and 68.07%. That is 2.46076×10^9 nominal solar luminosities, IAU 3.828×10^26 W. The 0.6 is Timmes, Brown, and Truran 2003, a fiducial from average peak magnitudes, approximate, not one named supernova. SN 1987A is 0.071 solar masses, the mass Suntzeff and Bouchet 1990 use, with their range 0.055–0.090. Arnett and Fu 1989 fit 0.073 ± 0.015. The button is 0.071. The two fits are not averaged. By day 800 of SN 1987A, Suntzeff and Bouchet say more than half the bolometric flux was escaping as high-energy photons. This page does not remove that leak. The distance-ladder candle stays M_B = −19.25 from Richardson et al. 2014. Hillebrandt and Niemeyer’s −19.30 is the value at H0 = 60. It is not substituted. Arnett’s rule is named and not given a day. Not a light-curve fit.

entries.title: Accretion and the Eddington limit
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an accretion page. The Eddington luminosity for a sphere of pure ionized hydrogen, with Thomson scattering as the only opacity, is L_Edd = 4π G M m_p c / σ_T. σ_T is the 2022 CODATA Thomson cross section, 6.6524587051 × 10^−29 m². The proton mass is 1.67262192595 × 10^−27 kg. G is 6.67430 × 10^−11. c is 299,792,458 m/s exactly. A solar mass is the IAU 2015 nominal GM☉, 1.3271244 × 10^20, divided by that G. One solar mass computes 1.25707 × 10^31 W, which is 3.28387 × 10^4 nominal solar luminosities. A familiar round figure is 1.26 × 10^31 W. 1.25707 × 10^31 rounds to that at three figures. The calculator uses the arithmetic. L = ε Ṁ c². The default ε is 0.1. The Schwarzschild ISCO binding energy is 1 − √(8/9) = 0.0571910. The maximal prograde Kerr closed form on the button is 1 − 1/√3 = 0.422650. Familiar round figures are 0.057 and 0.42. They are not substituted. This page does not integrate a Kerr geodesic. At ε = 0.1 and λ = 1 the supply rate is 1.39867 × 10^15 kg/s, which is 2.21980 × 10^−8 solar masses per Julian year. The e-folding time is ε/(1−ε) × σ_T c / (4π G m_p) / λ. At those sliders it is 5.00545 × 10^7 Julian years. The product that drops (1−ε) and keeps only ε is 4.50490 × 10^7 years. A familiar round figure is about 45 million years, from that shorter product. The calculator uses ε/(1−ε). The two times are not averaged. Salpeter 1964 is the name on the clock. From 100 solar masses to 10^9 the count is ln(10^7) = 16.1181 e-folds, and the time at ε = 0.1 and λ = 1 is 8.06783 × 10^8 years. That span is a classroom seed. It is not a named quasar. Cygnus X-1 is 21.2 ± 2.2 solar masses, Miller-Jones et al. 2021. Sagittarius A* is 4.297 × 10^6 solar masses, GRAVITY Collaboration 2022. M87* is 6.5 × 10^9 solar masses, EHT 2019 Paper VI. The points are L_Edd at those central values, not the light we measure. Each preset is approximate. Real disks can exceed L_Edd. Not a disk model.

entries.title: Star-formation desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a star-formation page. A cold molecular cloud collapses when gravity beats thermal pressure. This page uses the uniform-sphere virial line 2K = |U|, with gravitational energy (3/5) G M^2/R and thermal energy (3/2) N k T. The Jeans mass is M_J = (5 k T / (G μ m_H))^(3/2) * (3 / (4 π ρ))^(1/2), with ρ = n μ m_H. The Jeans length is the critical radius R_J = (15 k T / (4 π G μ m_H ρ))^(1/2). The free-fall time is t_ff = (3 π / (32 G ρ))^(1/2). Rice University ASTR 350 notes of 28 October 2021 print this mass and call R_J the Jeans length. University of Toronto AST 320 notes print 29 solar masses and 0.30 pc at μ = 1, T = 10 K, and n = 10^4 per cm^3. This page’s arithmetic there is 29.1845 solar masses and 0.304295 pc. 29.1845 rounds to 29. 0.304295 rounds to 0.30. They are not averaged. The notes do not print the constants behind 29. The wavelength form (π k T / (G μ m_H ρ))^(1/2) is longer. The ratio of the two lengths is √15 / (2 π) = 0.616404. It is not substituted. k is exact, 1.380649 × 10^−23. G is the 2022 CODATA central value, 6.67430 × 10^−11. The proton mass is 1.67262192595 × 10^−27 kg and the electron mass is 9.1093837139 × 10^−31 kg. Their sum, the hydrogen mass on this page, is 1.67353286432 × 10^−27 kg. The 13.6 eV binding energy is omitted. A solar mass is the IAU 2015 nominal GM☉, 1.3271244 × 10^20, divided by that G, which is 1.9884098707 × 10^30 kg. One parsec is (648000/π) au, 3.085677581491 × 10^16 m. A year is the Julian year, 31,557,600 s. At 10 K, n = 10^4 per cm^3, and μ = 2.33, the arithmetic is 5.37577 solar masses, 0.130599 pc, and 337.100 thousand years. The unrounded time is 337099.930 years. The four buttons are typical textbook values. Diffuse atomic gas, 100 K, 10 per cm^3, μ = 1.3, is 1.72690 × 10^4 solar masses. A giant molecular cloud, 10 K, 100 per cm^3, μ = 2.33, is 53.7577 solar masses. Warm H II gas, 10,000 K, 100 per cm^3, μ = 0.6, is 2.56360 × 10^7 solar masses. They are not measurements of a named cloud. NASA Science says molecular clouds range from 1,000 to 10 million times the mass of the Sun. That range is not this formula. They are not averaged. At fixed temperature, M_J falls as n^−1/2, which is why an isothermal cloud fragments into a cluster. If the gas cannot cool, M_J rises as T^3/2. Classroom uniform-sphere picture, not a simulation of a cloud.

entries.title: Tidal-locking desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a tidal-locking page. A tidal bulge that leads the partner slows a spin; a bulge that lags speeds it up; synchronous rotation puts the bulge on the line of centers. The order-of-magnitude time is t_lock = (ω a^6 I Q) / (3 G m_p^2 k2 R^5), with I = f m_s R^2. It is the inversion of Hinkel and Kane 2013, ApJ 774, 27, equation (2). They set k2 = 0.3 and I ≈ 0.4 M R^2, and, citing Kasting et al. 1993, one rotation per 13.5 hours and Q = 100. They attribute the expression to Peale 1977 and Gladman et al. 1996, Icarus 122, 166. This page has not re-read those two. Cuartas-Restrepo et al., arXiv:1606.07546, equation (5), print twice this time and also cite Gladman. The factor of two is not substituted. G is the 2022 CODATA central value, 6.67430 × 10^−11. A year is the Julian year, 31,557,600 s. Moon–Earth uses the Moon sheet’s 0.07346 × 10^24 kg, 1,737.4 km, I/MR^2 = 0.394, and 0.3844 × 10^6 km, and the Earth sheet’s 5.9722 × 10^24 kg. The Moon sheet’s Earth column, 5.9724 × 10^24 kg, is not substituted. The 655.720 hour rotation is the locked state, not the initial spin. With the assumed 13.5 hours, Q = 100, and k2 = 0.3, the arithmetic is 3.40464 million years. Half that distance is 53.1974 thousand years, the time divided by 64. Io–Jupiter uses 893.2 × 10^20 kg, 1,821.5 km, and 421.8 × 10^3 km, with Jupiter’s 1,898.13 × 10^24 kg. The sheet prints no I/MR^2, so f = 0.4 is assumed. The time is 63.0232 years. Mercury–Sun uses 0.33010 × 10^24 kg, 2,439.7 km, I/MR^2 = 0.35, and 57.909 × 10^6 km, with the Sun’s 1,988,400 × 10^24 kg. The J2000 axis 0.38709893 AU is not substituted. 1407.6 hours and 87.969 days are 1.4999 orbits per sidereal rotation, near 3/2, not exactly 3/2. NASA Science calls that a 3:2 resonance. It is not 1:1. The time, 517.565 million years, is a despinning time toward synchronous rotation, not a capture time. Proxima Cen b uses the NASA Exoplanet Archive composite row: minimum mass 1.055 M⊕, radius 1.02 R⊕ with a null error, 0.04848 AU, and stellar mass 0.1221 M☉. NASA Science’s card matches those three and calls the radius an estimate. The sentence on that card says 1.07 Earths, 11.2 days, and 0.04856 AU. They are not averaged. R⊕ is the Earth sheet’s 6,371.000 km. M☉ is the Sun sheet’s mass. f = 0.4 is assumed. The time is 154.634 thousand years. Pluto’s sidereal rotation is −153.2928 hours. 153.2928 / 24 = 6.3872 days, the Charon block’s orbit and rotation. NASA Science calls that mutual tidal locking. The formula is not run for the pair. Order of magnitude only. Q and k2 are very uncertain. Not a tidal-evolution model.

entries.title: Rotation-curve desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a rotation-curve page. Circular speed is v = sqrt(G M(<r) / r). A central mass falls as r^−1/2. A flat curve means enclosed mass grows about linearly with r. Rubin and Ford 1970 measured 67 H II regions in M31 from 3 to 24 kpc. Their abstract says the mass beyond 4 kpc increases approximately linearly to 14 kpc, and the mass to 24 kpc is (1.85 ± 0.1) × 10^11 solar masses. They are not refit. G is the 2022 CODATA central value, 6.67430 × 10^−11. A solar mass is the IAU 2015 nominal GM☉, 1.3271244 × 10^20, divided by that G, which is 1.9884098707 × 10^30 kg. In solar masses G cancels and M = v²r/GM☉. One parsec is (648000/π) au, IAU 2015 Resolution B2 footnote 4, with the 2012 au of 149,597,870,700 m, so 1 pc is 3.085677581491 × 10^16 m. GRAVITY Collaboration 2019 print R0 = 8178 ± 13 statistical ± 22 systematic pc. Eilers et al. 2019 print 229.0 ± 0.2 km/s. They adopted 8.122 ± 0.031 kpc. 8.178 − 8.122 = 0.056 kpc. Their slope is −1.7 km/s per kpc. 0.056 × 1.7 = 0.0952 km/s. This page does not subtract it. P = 2πR/v with a Julian year of 31,557,600 s. The unrounded period is 219.400731 Myr, which rounds to 219.401 Myr. The enclosed mass is 9.971419 × 10^10 solar masses. The 2021 GRAVITY value 8275 pc is not substituted. The Milky Way button is a classroom toy: bulge 1 × 10^10 solar masses at 0.5 kpc, disk 5 × 10^10 at 3 kpc, halo 180 km/s with rc = 5 kpc. At 8.178 kpc that toy is 193.039 km/s and 260.273 Myr. 193.039 does not round to 229.0. They are not averaged. Milgrom 1983 is named and not drawn. Not a mass model and not a fit.

entries.title: Radial-velocity desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a radial-velocity page. K = (2πG/P)^(1/3) · m_p sin i / (M* + m_p)^(2/3) / √(1−e²). G is the 2022 CODATA central value, 6.67430 × 10^−11. A solar mass, an Earth mass, and a Jupiter mass are the NSSDCA fact-sheet masses. The sheet’s GM is not substituted. Sun–Jupiter, period 4,332.589 days and e = 0.0487, edge-on, computes 12.47 m/s. With e set to 0 it is 12.46 m/s. A familiar round figure is about 12.5 m/s. 12.47 does not round to 12.5. Sun–Earth computes 0.0895 m/s, which is 8.95 cm/s. The unrounded value is 0.089471 m/s. The fact-sheet inclinations, 1.304° and 0.000°, are to the ecliptic and are not the line of sight. 51 Pegasi b uses the archive composite cited to Cont et al. 2026: the arithmetic is 55.95 m/s beside the listed 55.77 ± 0.15 m/s. They are not averaged. Proxima Centauri b uses Suárez Mascareño et al. 2025. The row is m sin i, 1.055 ± 0.055 M⊕, and the inclination is null, so this page sets 90°. The arithmetic is 1.2257 m/s, which rounds to the listed 1.226 m/s at three decimals. GJ 436 b uses Maciejewski et al. 2014, 22.1 M⊕ and e = 0.13827. The arithmetic is 17.04 m/s beside 17.09 ± 0.22 m/s. The curve solves Kepler’s equation. HARPS’s ESO overview says about 1 m/s RMS for a stated class of star. ESPRESSO’s overview lists a requirement below 10 cm/s in the 1-UT high-resolution mode. Those sentences are not a detection threshold. Not a measured orbit.

entries.title: Barycenter desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a barycenter page. r₁ = a · m₂ / (m₁ + m₂) and r₂ = a · m₁ / (m₁ + m₂). The unrounded distances add to a. Earth–Moon uses the Earth sheet’s 5.9722 × 10^24 kg, not the Moon sheet’s Earth column of 5.9724 × 10^24 kg, the Moon’s 0.07346 × 10^24 kg, and the semimajor axis 0.3844 × 10^6 km. The arithmetic is 4,670.8 km from Earth’s center and 379,729.2 km from the Moon’s. Earth’s volumetric mean radius is 6,371.000 km. The ratio is 0.733, inside Earth. The Moon’s eccentricity 0.0549 stays, so a is not the distance today. Sun–Jupiter uses 1,988,400 × 10^24 kg, 1,898.13 × 10^24 kg, and 778.479 × 10^6 km. The arithmetic is 742,428.6 km, ratio 1.067, which is 1.07 at two decimals, outside the 695,700 km volumetric radius. The gap is 46,728.6 km. The sheet’s photosphere thickness is ~500 km and is not subtracted. Sun–Earth is 449.3 km, ratio 0.000646, inside the Sun. The Earth sheet’s 1.00000011 AU is not substituted for 149.598 × 10^6 km. Pluto–Charon uses 0.01303 × 10^24 kg, 1.586 × 10^21 kg, and the mean distance from Pluto, 19,596 km. The arithmetic is 2,126.4 km, ratio 1.790, outside the 1,188 km radius. Charon’s eccentricity is 0.0. The barycentric sentence under Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra is not applied to that 19,596 km. Alpha Centauri uses Akeson et al. 2021 Table 8. 17.4930 / 0.75081 is 23.298837 AU, the same axis as the binary-stars desk, split into 10.655585 AU and 12.643252 AU, outside both radii. The Sun sheet’s printed mass ratio 332,900 is not the division 1,988,400 / 5.9722 = 332,942.63. The Lagrange desk rounds three of these splits to 4,671 km, 449 km, and 742,429 km. The tenth stays. They are not averaged. The lower drawing is an approximate schematic: the solar map’s helio places from 2000 through 2050, every 20 days, weighted by the fact-sheet masses. At J2000 the distance is 1,146,642 km, 1.648 volumetric radii, outside the Sun. The sample runs from 93,388.7 km to 1,377,647 km, 345 points inside and 569 outside. That count is the sample. It is not a fraction of all time. The two-body Sun–Jupiter line is a different sum. Not an ephemeris and not a JPL Horizons barycenter.

entries.title: Density desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a density page. Mean density is ρ = M / (4/3 π R³). Surface gravity on the side is g = G M / R², with the 2022 CODATA G times the printed mass. The sheet’s GM is not substituted. Planet sheets use the volumetric mean radius. Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, and Titan use the one radius on the satellite sheet. Earth’s arithmetic is 5513.4 kg/m³, which is 5.5134 g/cm³. The Earth sheet prints 5513. 5513.4 rounds to 5513. They are not averaged. The comparison table, updated 13 November 2026, prints 5,514. The Moon sheet’s Earth column prints 5.9724 × 10^24 kg and 5514. This page uses 5.9722 × 10^24 kg and 5513. Mercury’s 5426.8 does not round to 5429. Pluto’s 1855.3 does not round to 1854. The comparison table’s 1,850 is not substituted. Io’s 3528.4 does not round to 3530. Europa’s 3013.8 does not round to 3010. Ganymede’s 1942.1 does not round to 1940. Callisto’s 1834.3 does not round to 1830. Titan’s 1881.3 does not round to 1880. Titan’s g is 1.354 m/s², the same figure the scale-height desk computes, and the satellite sheet still prints no gravity. Saturn’s arithmetic is 687.1 kg/m³ beside the sheet’s 687. Both are below 1,000 kg/m³. NASA Science says Saturn is the only planet with an average density less than water. Jupiter’s sheet is 1,326 kg/m³. NASA Science says pressure inside Jupiter compresses hydrogen into a liquid. An uncompressed density is the materials with that squeeze taken off. The fact sheets do not print one. This page does not invent one. The water line is 1 g/cm³. The rock mark at 3 and the iron mark at 7.9 are reference marks, not fact-sheet densities. Classroom bulk-density picture, not an interior model.

entries.title: Scale height desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a scale-height page. H = kT/(m g) = R T/(M g), and P(z) = P0·exp(−z/H). The temperature, mean molecular weight, and mean gravity are the NSSDCA fact-sheet lines. Earth’s arithmetic is 8.417 km. The Earth sheet prints 8.5 km. 8.417 does not round to 8.5. They are not averaged. The defined standard acceleration, 9.80665 m/s², stays out of the formula. The mean surface gravity 9.820 is the one used. The comparison table’s 9.8 is not substituted. Venus’s 15.900 rounds to the sheet’s 15.9 at one decimal. Mars’s 10.969 rounds to 11.0, and the tilde on ~214 K stays. Jupiter is 23.841 km beside 27 km, Saturn 48.099 beside 59.5, Uranus 26.566 beside 27.7. Those gravities and temperatures are the 1-bar lines. Neptune’s molecular weight is 2.53–2.69 and the scale height is 19.1–20.3 km. The arithmetic at the two ends is 20.995 km and 19.747 km. The ends are not averaged. Titan’s satellite sheet prints mass 1,345.5 × 10^20 kg and radius 2,575 km, and does not print g, T, M, or a scale height. GM/r² with the 2022 CODATA G is 1.354 m/s². The same 288 K and 28.97 at that gravity give 61.030 km, 7.251 times Earth’s 8.417 km, because H is inversely proportional to g. That curve is the low g. It is not a Titan atmosphere from the sheet. Classroom isothermal model, not a climate model.

entries.title: Magnetospheres desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a magnetospheres page. The nose is a Chapman–Ferraro pressure balance, R_mp/R = (k B² / (2 μ0 ρ v²))^(1/6), with k = 2 multiplying B². k = 2 is this page’s assumption for a dipole compressed by the solar wind. It is not a doubling of the field, and it is not a measured factor. B is the fact sheet’s dipole field strength. Mercury 0.002 Gauss-Rh³, Earth 0.306 Gauss-Re³, Jupiter 4.30 Gauss-Rj³, Saturn 0.215 Gauss-Rs³, Uranus 0.228 Gauss-Ru³, Neptune 0.142 Gauss-Rn³. The surface ranges stay beside those lines and are not substituted. Model radii stay beside the equatorial radii and are not averaged: Earth 6,378 km beside 6378.137 km, Jupiter 71,398 km beside 71,492 km. Density at 1 AU opens on the NOAA glossary’s near 5 protons per cm³. Speed opens on NOAA’s about 400 km/s, the same sentence as Marshall’s about 400. The glossary’s near 375 km/s is a different button. SPARTAN’s about 3 to 10 per cm³ contains the 5 and is not averaged with it. Density at the planet is divided by the square of the J2000 semimajor axis. Speed is not scaled. Earth’s density at 1.00000011 AU is 4.999999 per cm³, not exactly 5. Earth’s arithmetic is 9.070 Re. NOAA NCEI says about 10 Earth radii. NASA Science says about six to 10. 9.070 is inside that span and does not round to 10. They are not averaged. The Earth sheet prints no dipole tilt. Mercury’s arithmetic is 1.236 Rh. Winslow et al. 2013 print 1.45 RM at 14.3 nPa. This page’s pressure there is 8.9298 nPa. Jupiter’s arithmetic is 37.929 Rj. Bagenal 2024 prints a dipolar stand-off of about 42 RJ, typical sunward distances of 63 to 92 RJ, and also 60 to 100, with RJ = 71,492 km. Saturn’s arithmetic is 17.100 Rs, beside the Cassini report’s about 22 and about 27. The sheet’s tilt is 0.0, and the sheet spells quadrapole. Uranus is 22.016 Ru beside Paty et al. 2020’s 18 RU, tilt 58.6°, offset 0.352 Ru. Neptune is 21.837 Rn beside 23 to 26 RN, tilt 46.9°, offset 0.485 Rn. A GSFC page’s about 60° for both ice giants is not those sheet tilts. Venus has an induced magnetic field on the NASA Venus facts page. Mars has remnant fossil crustal fields and no global dipole. The formula is not run for either. Io’s about one ton per second, and a later over a ton per second, are Bagenal’s and are not averaged. Ganymede is the only moon NASA Science says has its own magnetic field. Simplified pressure-balance model, not mission-grade.

entries.title: Temperatures desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a temperatures page. The fast-rotator equilibrium temperature is T_eq = [L(1−A)/(16πσd²)]^(1/4), emissivity 1. L is the Sun fact sheet’s 382.8 × 10^24 W. A is the Bond albedo on each body’s sheet. d is the J2000 semimajor axis, except the Moon, whose sheet prints Earth’s irradiance 1361.0 W/m² and no heliocentric axis. The Moon’s 0.3844 × 10^6 km is the Earth–Moon distance and is not d. The slow button replaces the 4 with a 2 and does not rewrite the sheet’s black-body temperature. The greenhouse blanket is a drawing and is not a term. Earth’s arithmetic is 255.1 K. The Earth sheet prints a black-body temperature of 254.0 K and an average of 288 K. 288 minus 254.0 is 34. 288 minus 255.1 is 32.9. They are not averaged. Venus’s arithmetic matches 226.6 K, and 737 minus 226.6 is 510.4. Mars’s ~214 minus 209.8 is 4.2. The tilde stays. Mercury’s arithmetic is 439.5 K beside the sheet’s 439.6 K, and 440 minus 439.6 is 0.4, which is not read as a greenhouse excess. The Moon’s sheet prints no average, so that cell is a dash. The diurnal range is 95 K to 390 K. The comparison table’s −20 °C is not subtracted from 270.4. Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune match their black-body temperatures at the printed tenth on the luminosity path. Jupiter’s irradiance path rounds to 109.8 K, one tenth below 109.9. Saturn’s luminosity path is 81.2 K. The irradiance path rounds to the sheet’s 81.0 K. Pluto’s arithmetic is 32.2 K. The sheet prints 37.5 K. The formula with Bond albedo 0.72 does not return 37.5. Giant-planet 1-bar gaps are not greenhouse excesses. NASA Science, 17 July 2025, says Jupiter, Saturn, and Neptune emit more energy than they receive, and that Uranus releases about 15% more, far less than Neptune’s more than twice. Those ratios are not the kelvin subtraction. Classroom energy-balance model, not a climate model.

entries.title: Obliquity desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an obliquity page. The spin axis is tipped from the orbit normal. Eight planets and Pluto, or a custom angle from 0° to 180°. Up to 90°, tropics sit at the obliquity and polar circles at 90 minus that angle. Past 90° the seasonal swing on the drawing is 180 minus the obliquity. The Venus sheet prints 177.36° and an equator inclination of 2.64°. The Uranus sheet prints 97.77° and 82.23°. Those pairs match the subtraction. The Pluto sheet prints 119.51° and 57.47°, and 180 − 119.51 is 60.49, which is not 57.47. They are not averaged. Saturn’s sheet does not print an equator inclination. The comparison table of 18 March 2025 prints the coarser cells, including Pluto 119.5 and a Moon cell of 6.7 that this desk does not use. NASA Science says Earth’s obliquity has varied between 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over the last million years, currently 23.4 on that page, in a cycle of about 41,000 years. The Earth sheet prints 23.44. They are not averaged. A photojournal caption says the Moon’s gravity appears to have limited Earth’s tilt to small variations, and that Mars’ obliquity probably reaches above 60 degrees and below 10. The Mars sheet’s present value is 25.19. Not an ephemeris.

entries.title: Planet days desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a planet-days page. A solar day is noon to the next noon. A sidereal rotation is one turn against the stars. The formula is 1/T_solar = 1/T_sidereal − 1/T_orbit. The sidereal orbit period is converted to hours by × 24, the Earth sheet’s length of day, 24.0000. Venus and Uranus print a minus sign, and that minus sign flips the first term. Each planet’s fact-sheet length of day stays beside the arithmetic. They are not averaged. Earth computes 24.000028 hours beside the printed 24.0000. Mercury computes 4223.376 hours beside the printed 4222.6, which does not round to 4222.6. That arithmetic is 2.0004 sidereal orbits, about two Mercury years. The printed periods are 1.4999 orbits per sidereal rotation, near 3/2, not exactly 3/2. Jupiter’s 9.9250 hours is marked System III (1965.0) coordinates. Saturn’s 10.656 hours is marked Saturnian System III coordinates. Uranus’s −17.24 hours and Neptune’s 16.11 hours are marked magnetic coordinates from the Voyager 2 radio science experiment. The length of day lines do not repeat those asterisks. The comparison table prints Venus’s rotation as −5832.5 hours. The Venus sheet prints −5832.6. They are not averaged. The comparison table’s orbital period is the tropical year. The formula uses the sidereal orbit period. Not an ephemeris.

entries.title: Frost line desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a frost-line page. The papers call the boundary the snow line. Hartmann, Ciesla, Gressel, and Alexander 2017 print Hayashi’s 1981 temperature as 280 K times (r / 1 AU) to the power −1/2. At 170 K that computes 2.713 AU. Podolak 2009, and Sasselov and Lecar 2000, print 2.7 AU for that step. The two figures are not averaged. Podolak prints 150 to 180 K depending on density. Hartmann and coauthors print about 120 to 170 K. The ice slider walks those ends and is not a pressure measurement. The scale multiplies the 280 K. It is a teaching knob, not a measured disk and not a young-Sun luminosity. Other printed distances stay in a table: greater than 1–3 AU, the neighborhood of 1 AU, beyond 4 AU, about 2 AU and as far as 3 AU, around 5 AU, the neighborhood of 10 AU, the middle of the asteroid belt, and perhaps at least one billion miles. NASA Science says less than one percent of Earth’s mass is water, and that even that may have been delivered by comets and asteroids. Planet marks are NSSDCA J2000 semimajor axes. Densities are the bulk-parameter lines: Mercury 5429, Venus 5243, Earth 5513, Mars 3934, Jupiter 1,326, Saturn 687, Uranus 1,270, Neptune 1,638. The comparison table’s 5,514 for Earth is a different printing. Jupiter’s ratio column 5.204, Saturn’s 9.573, and Neptune’s 30.178 are not averaged with the J2000 lines. The band between Mars and Jupiter is the asteroids desk. Not a disk model.

entries.title: Interstellar desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an interstellar page. The slider runs eccentricity from 0 to 6.5, so a circle becomes an ellipse, a parabola at e = 1, then a hyperbola. The signed axis is a = q / (1 − e). Vis-viva at infinite distance is v∞² = GM (e − 1) / q, with the Sun Fact Sheet GM, 132,712 × 10^6 km³/s². Below e = 1 there is no v∞. 1I/‘Oumuamua is JPL solution 16: e = 1.201133796102373, q = 0.2559115812959116 AU, orbit class Hyperbolic Asteroid. The computed excess speed is 26.405 km/s. NASA Science says it was discovered on 19 October 2017, showed no cometary activity after perihelion, and later a slight acceleration. 2I/Borisov is JPL solution 54: e = 3.356475782676596, q = 2.006520878500843 AU, Hyperbolic Comet, computed v∞ = 32.278 km/s. NASA Science says Gennady Borisov found it on 30 August 2019 and that it developed a coma. 3I/ATLAS is JPL solution 55: e = 6.123467394525528, q = 1.351998619400212 AU, Hyperbolic Comet, computed v∞ = 57.981 km/s. JPL calls that solution temporary, for JWST Program 13145. NASA Science says ATLAS reported it on 1 July 2025 and that the path does not close. ESA’s Comet Interceptor, launch late 2028 or early 2029, lists a pristine comet or an interstellar object as the destination. Not a JPL Horizons ephemeris.

entries.title: Planetary rings desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a rings page for Saturn, Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune. Distances are kilometers from the planet’s center, from the NSSDCA ring fact sheets. An edge the sheet does not print is a dash. The fluid Roche distance uses 2.44 and the rigid distance uses 1.26, with the volumetric mean radius, the same formulas as the Roche desk. Saturn at equal density is 142,086 km and 73,372 km. Rhea’s 1,240 kg/m³, the Roche desk’s pair, is 116,698 km and 60,262 km. The Mimas 2:1 uses Mimas’s semimajor axis, 185.52 × 10^3 km, and Saturn’s GM, 37.931 × 10^6 km^3/s^2. Kepler’s third law gives 116,870 km, which is 637 km inside the B ring’s outer edge at 117,507 km. The Cassini division row has no radius. NASA Science gives the division’s width as 4,700 km on the Saturn facts page and 4,800 km on a Cassini caption. Those widths are not averaged. Prometheus, Pandora, Cordelia, Ophelia, and Galatea are marked from the satellite sheets where a NASA page cites their effect on a ring. A Cassini mass page says the findings indicate an age between 10 million and 100 million years. An Ames page says the age has been hard to pin down and that the exposure is not more than a few hundred million years. This desk does not pick an age. Not an ephemeris.

entries.title: Ocean worlds desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an ocean-worlds page. The cutaway switches among Europa, Enceladus, Ganymede, Callisto, and Titan, with Triton and Pluto as dashed candidates. Fact-sheet radii and periods: Europa 1,560.8 km and 3.551181 days, Enceladus 257 × 251 × 248 km and 1.370218 days, Ganymede 2,631.2 km and 7.154553 days, Callisto 2,410.3 km and 16.689017 days, Titan 2,575 km and 15.945421 days, Triton 1,353.4 km and 5.876854 days retrograde, Pluto 1,188 km and 90,560 days around the Sun. Ice and ocean cells use published ranges: Europa about 15–25 km and about 60–150 km on the Clipper FAQ, and about 29 km in the Juno region; Enceladus about 30–40 km and about 10 km under the south pole; Ganymede about 150 km and about 100 km, called estimates. Callisto’s ocean depth, Titan’s thicknesses, and both thicknesses for Triton and Pluto are dashes. The slider is eccentricity only. Flex follows e. Heating follows e², with Europa’s 0.009 as 1. Europa over Io is 2.007295. Dione over Enceladus is 1.997430. Europa Clipper launched 14 October 2024 and is not a life-detection mission. Juice arrives at Jupiter in July 2031. Dragonfly is no earlier than July 2028. Not to scale.

entries.title: Asteroid belt desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an asteroid-belt page. The histogram runs from 2.0 to 3.5 AU and is a schematic: every full bar is the same height, and a notch one bin wide, 0.025 AU, marks a computed Kirkwood axis. Bar height is not a count. Jupiter’s fact-sheet J2000 axis is 5.20336301 AU and the sidereal period is 4,332.589 days. The 4:1 computes 2.064956 AU, the 3:1 computes 2.501516 AU, the 5:2 computes 2.824820 AU, the 7:3 computes 2.957783 AU, and the 2:1 computes 3.277913 AU. JPL’s June 2007 histogram labels 3:1, 5:2, 7:3, and 2:1. It does not label the 4:1. The 3:2 Hilda axis is 3.970909 AU. The 1:1 is 5.20336301 AU. Ceres, Vesta, Pallas, and Hygiea use JPL Small-Body Database solutions 48, 36, 74, and 129. NASA Science says the total mass of all the asteroids combined is less than that of Earth’s Moon. Not an ephemeris.

entries.title: Dwarf planets desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a dwarf-planet page. The map is a top-down view of the ecliptic. Neptune’s ellipse is the fact-sheet J2000 block, 30.06896348 AU. An exact 3:2 on that axis is 39.401489 AU, and an exact 2:1 is 47.731504 AU. Pluto’s own J2000 axis is 39.48168677 AU, eccentricity 0.24880766, period 90,560 days. The circle is 2,376 km, twice the fact-sheet radius of 1,188 km. Ceres, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris use JPL Small-Body Database solutions 48, 132, 130, and 103. NASA Science lists five dwarf planets and puts the classical Kuiper belt’s average distance between about 40 and 50 AU. The shade is that sentence. IAU Resolution 5A is the three criteria: orbit the Sun, nearly round, and clear the neighbourhood. A dwarf planet has not cleared it, and is not a satellite. Symbols sit at perihelion. Not a JPL Horizons ephemeris.

entries.title: Solar wind and CME desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a solar-wind and coronal-mass-ejection page. The slider walks NOAA’s CME range, from slower than 250 km/s to near 3,000 km/s. Marks at 300, 400, 500, and 800 km/s are the solar-wind sentences: Marshall’s 300 km/s over streamers and 800 km/s over coronal holes, NOAA’s about 400 km/s in the equatorial plane and 500 to 800 km/s from coronal holes, and NASA SVS’s slow band of about 300–500 km/s and fast band of about 500–800 km/s. The time is the Earth Fact Sheet semimajor axis, 149.598 × 10^6 km, divided by the selected speed. At about 400 km/s that division is 103.89 hours, 4.33 days. It is not NOAA’s 15–18 hours and not NASA’s as little as 15 hours. The Earth-directed and glancing buttons move a cartoon. They are not an angle. The spiral is a sketch of NASA’s Parker sentence and NOAA’s 27-day ballerina skirt. No angle is computed. Not a forecast, not a Kp or G-scale predictor, and not a live catalog.

entries.title: Aurora desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an aurora page. Earth’s magnetic field is drawn as a dipole-like shield. NASA Science says the dayside magnetosphere extends about six to 10 Earth radii, and the nightside tail can measure hundreds of Earth radii, past the Moon at 60. The slider only walks that span, outer end first. NOAA’s glossary puts about 2 Earth radii of magnetosheath along the Sun–Earth axis, and the bow shock is that thickness stacked on the slider. Under average conditions the same glossary puts the oval at about 75° magnetic latitude at local noon and about 67° at midnight. The circle is fitted to those two latitudes. The storm sketch slides it 12° equatorward. Twelve degrees is a classroom offset, not a storm latitude and not a Kp index. NOAA NCEI’s WMM2020 inclination, 9.41°, is the angle in the drawing. The same page’s opening answer says approximately 11°, and SWPC’s glossary says about 11.5°. They are not averaged. Green oxygen is NASA’s about 100–200 km. The column stops at 500 km. No wavelengths are listed. Not a forecast.

entries.title: Van Allen belts desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a Van Allen belts page. A noon–midnight cut shows the inner and outer toruses and a labeled slot. NASA’s 22 December 2021 Webb note is the span the sliders walk: the inner belt about 400 to 6,000 miles (about 650 to 9,660 kilometers), the outer belt 8,400 to 36,000 miles (about 13,500 to 60,000 kilometers). Basics of Space Flight centers the inner region about 3,000 km up and the outer belt about 15,000 to 20,000 km up. Those are presets, not an average with the ends. The station mark is NASA Science’s roughly 250 miles (400 km). The satellites desk’s about 420 km is a different sentence and is not used. The column breaks at 10,000 km and stops at 65,000 km so the picture can be read. Those two numbers are not belt edges. The South Atlantic Anomaly is a cited note. No dip distance is drawn. Not a radiation forecast, not a dose calculator, and not a live belt model.

entries.title: Comets desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a comet page. The path is a bound ellipse, a = q / (1 − e), and the place comes from Kepler’s equation. Speed is vis-viva with the Sun Fact Sheet GM, 132,712 × 10^6 km³/s². The ion tail is drawn straight away from the Sun. The dust tail lags along the orbit and is pushed outward. Both lengths grow as heliocentric distance shrinks, on a classroom scale. The 3 AU mark is the distance past which Cochran, McKay, and Moulane 2025 say water ice stays frozen. 1P/Halley is JPL orbit solution 75: q = 0.5748638313743413 AU, e = 0.9679359956953211, a = 17.92863504856923 AU. Perihelion speed computes 55.108 km/s. The two-body period is 75.914 years, beside JPL’s printed 27,728.046 days. 2P/Encke is solution K273/27, q = 0.3394588840071771 AU, e = 0.846979230409067. 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko is solution K284/1, q = 1.243265640702404 AU, e = 0.6409081308996354. C/1995 O1 (Hale–Bopp) is solution 226, q = 0.890537663547794 AU, e = 0.9949810027633206, period about 2,363.496 years. Inclination is printed and not drawn. Not a JPL Horizons ephemeris and not a tail model.

entries.title: Solar cycle desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a solar-cycle page. The numbers are SILSO version 2.0, fetched 5 November 2026: monthly means from January 1749 through October 2026, and the 13-month smoothed series. Cycle edges are the minimum months in SILSO’s TableCyclesMiMa.csv. The peak and the length are read from the smoothed series. Cycle 19’s smoothed peak is 285.0 in March 1958, and the length is 10 years 6 months. Cycle 24’s minimum is December 2008 at 2.2, the peak is 116.4 in April 2014, and the length is 11 years. Cycle 25’s minimum is December 2019 at 1.8. In this snapshot the highest smoothed value since then is 160.9 in October 2024, and that month is definitive. The downloadable cycle table leaves the maximum blank. The cycles min/max page, fetched the same day, prints October 2024 and 160.9. Later smoothed months are lower, through the provisional April 2026 value of 88.6. The length is not known. The highest monthly mean in the cycle is 216.0 in August 2024. The Sun drawing is a schematic of the equatorward drift, not a catalog. Not a forecast.

entries.title: Binary stars desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a binary-star page. The total mass is a³/P² in solar masses, AU, and years. The barycenter splits the axis. Each star’s circular speed is 2π a / P, and the radial-velocity semi-amplitude is that speed times |sin i| / √(1−e²). One AU in one year of 365.256 days is 29.785 km/s. Sirius uses Bond et al. 2017: 7.4957″, parallax 0.3789″, period 50.1284 yr. That axis is 19.782792 AU and a³/P² is 3.081024 solar masses, beside the paper’s 3.081 ± 0.034. Alpha Centauri uses Akeson et al. 2021, Table 8: 17.4930″ and 750.81 mas give 23.298837 AU and 1.987974 solar masses, beside 1.0788 + 0.9092 = 1.9880. Algol’s inner pair uses Kolbas et al. 2015: 3.39 and 0.770 solar masses, period 2.867328 days, i = 81.4°. The axis computes 13.660 R☉ beside 13.65 ± 0.07, and K computes 44.112 and 194.205 km/s beside 44.1 ± 0.2 and 194.2 ± 1.2. The light curve is two uniform disks. Algol C is omitted. Not an ephemeris and not a spectroscopic orbit fit.

entries.title: Orbital resonances desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a mean-motion resonance page. A p:q ratio means the inner body completes p orbits while the outer body completes q. Kepler’s third law maps that to distance: a₂/a₁ = (P₂/P₁) to the power 2/3. Jupiter’s fact sheet is 5.20336301 AU and 4,332.589 days. The 3:1 interior resonance computes 2.501516 AU and 1,444.196 days. The same formula places 5:2 at 2.824820 AU, 7:3 at 2.957783 AU, 2:1 at 3.277913 AU, and the 3:2 Hilda ratio at 3.970909 AU. JPL’s June 2007 histogram of 156,929 numbered asteroids labels gaps at 3:1, 5:2, 7:3, and 2:1. This page marks those computed locations and does not replot the counts. Io, Europa, and Ganymede use the Jovian Satellite Fact Sheet periods 1.769138, 3.551181, and 7.154553 days. Europa/Io computes 2.007295. Ganymede/Io computes 4.044090. The Laplace combination computes −1.41×10⁻⁷. NASA Science describes the pattern as one, two, and four. Neptune’s 60,189.018 days and Pluto’s 90,560 days give a printed period ratio of 1.504593, beside 3/2. An exact 3:2 on Neptune’s sheet computes 90,283.527 days and 39.401489 AU, beside Pluto’s printed 39.48168677 AU. TRAPPIST-1 periods are Agol et al. 2021, Table 2. Adjacent ratios are computed from those periods. Circular schematic. Not an ephemeris.

entries.title: Compact stars desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a compact-star page. A white dwarf’s radius is Nauenberg 1972, equations (54)–(56) with no magnetic energy: R/R☉ = (0.0225/μ_e) times the square root of 1 minus (M/M_Ch) to the 4/3, divided by (M/M_Ch) to the 1/3, and M_Ch/M☉ = 5.82/μ_e². For helium, carbon, or oxygen, μ_e = 2 and the limit is 1.455 M☉. Iron-56 uses 56/26 and the limit is 1.255 M☉. Sirius B is Bond et al. 2017, mass 1.018 ± 0.011 M☉. The relation gives 0.007800 R☉. The paper’s STIS radius is 0.008098 ± 0.000046 R☉, and this page’s log g from that mass and radius is 8.629, the figure Bond prints. Procyon B is Bond et al. 2015, mass 0.592 ± 0.006 M☉ and radius 0.01232 ± 0.00032 R☉. The relation gives 0.01269 R☉. This page’s log g from the published mass and radius is 8.029. Bond prints 8.028 ± 0.023. Neutron-star radii are not one equation of state. The band is Miller et al. 2021’s ±1σ span at 1.4 M☉ across three frameworks, 11.79–13.11 km. PSR J0030+0451 uses Riley et al. 2019 medians, 1.34 M☉ and 12.71 km. Compactness computed here is 0.156, the figure they print. PSR J0740+6620 uses Fonseca et al. 2021, 2.08 ± 0.07 M☉, and Riley et al. 2021, 12.39 km. Escape speed is the Newtonian square root of 2GM/R. A teaspoon mass is the density on the card times one US teaspoon, 4.92892159375 cm³. The spin is the pulsar desk. The horizon is the black-hole desk. Not a stellar model and not a dense-matter inference.

entries.title: Gravitational lensing desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a gravitational-lensing page. A point mass bends a light ray by α = 4GM/(c² b). c is 299,792,458 m/s exactly. One nominal solar mass uses the IAU 2015 GM☉, 1.3271244×10^20 m³/s², and the nominal solar radius 6.957×10^8 m, which is the Sun Fact Sheet’s 695,700 km. That limb ray computes 1.751″. Dyson, Eddington, and Davidson 1920 quote Einstein’s limb value as 1.75″ and the Newtonian half as 0.87″. This page’s half is 0.8756″. Their Sobral 4-inch result is 1.98″, probable error about 0.12″. Longair 2015 reads the Príncipe reductions as 1.61″ ± 0.31″. Jupiter’s fact-sheet limb is 16.64 mas, computed, not a quoted measurement. The Einstein radius uses θ_E = sqrt(4GM/c² × D_LS/(D_L D_S)) with D_LS = D_S − D_L, a flat small-angle line. It opens at 1 nominal solar mass, 4 kpc, and 8 kpc, which are round opening values, not a measured lens, and prints 1.009 mas. Two images follow θ± = (β ± sqrt(β² + 4 θ_E²))/2. Total magnification is A = (u² + 2)/(u sqrt(u² + 4)). At u = 0.5, A is 2.183. Aligned, the image is the ring and the point-source magnification is unbounded. The light curve is the Paczyński track. OGLE-2005-BLG-390 uses the survey single-lens fit, u_min = 0.332 and t_E = 11.735 days, which recomputes A = 3.135 beside the survey’s printed Amax of 3.136 ± 0.044. Beaulieu et al. 2006 is a planet, u0 = 0.359 ± 0.005 and t_E = 11.03 ± 0.11 days, and that deviation is not on the curve. The Einstein Cross and SDSS J1004+4112 are cited as published separations, 1.8″ and 14.62″, and are not loaded into the point-mass calculator. Not a cosmological lens model and not a photometric fit.

entries.title: Which gases can a world keep?
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a thermal-escape page. Escape speed is √(2GM/r). The most probable thermal speed is √(2kT/m). The mean speed is √(8kT/(π m)). Jeans’ λ is v_esc² / v_mp², which is GMm/(kT r). Catling and Zahnle’s rough rule says a gas is retained over geologic time if escape speed exceeds about six times the mean speed. Earth’s fact-sheet GM and volumetric radius give 11.186 km/s at the surface. At an exobase of about 500 km and 1000 K, escape is 10.771 km/s. Atomic hydrogen’s mean speed is 4.583 km/s, a ratio of 2.35, and λ is 7.03. Nitrogen is 12.4 times, λ 195. Oxygen is 13.2 times, λ 223. Titan’s nitrogen, at 150 K and about 1500 km up, is 6.24 times, just over the line. The Moon at the fact sheet’s 270.4 K black-body temperature is 5.25 times, under it. Pluto’s nitrogen at 65 K is under the line and still present, because ice resupplies it. The six-times line is an approximation. Sputtering, photochemical escape, hydrodynamic escape, and impact erosion are named and not calculated.

entries.title: Pulsar spin-down desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a pulsar page. The inputs are the spin period P and the period derivative Ṗ. Dipole braking fixes the index at 3, so the characteristic age is P divided by 2 Ṗ. The surface dipole field is 3.2×10^19 times the square root of P Ṗ, in gauss, with a moment of inertia of 10^45 g cm^2 and a radius of 10 km. Spin-down luminosity is 4 π squared times I times Ṗ over P cubed. The light cylinder is c P over 2 π, with c = 299,792,458 m/s. The four buttons are P0 and P1 printed by ATNF Pulsar Catalogue version 2.9.0. Crab B0531+21, from Lyne et al. 2015 at MJD 48442.5, is P = 0.0333924123 s and Ṗ = 4.20972×10^−13. That is a characteristic age of 1,257 yr and a field of 3.794×10^12 G. The supernova of 1054 is 972 years before 2026. Vela B0833−45, from Dodson et al. 2002 at the January 2000 glitch epoch, is 11.32 kyr. J0437−4715, from Reardon et al. 2024, is 1.592 Gyr. B1919+21, from Hobbs et al. 2004, is 15.72 Myr. The diagram is log P against log Ṗ, with lines of constant age and constant field. A dashed line is Harding’s constant-potential sketch at 10^12 V, labeled as an approximate death valley, not a fit. No other pulsars are plotted. Idealized dipole. Not a timing model.

entries.title: Time-dilation desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a time-dilation page. A circular orbit’s speed is the square root of GM over r. The moving clock is slow by the exact Lorentz rate, the square root of 1 minus v squared over c squared, minus 1. The gravitational term is the weak-field monopole, GM times (1/R minus 1/r) over c squared, against a clock at rest on the equatorial radius. GM is 3.986004418×10^14 m^3/s^2, the TCG-compatible value in IERS Conventions (2010) Table 1.1, which is the value Ashby 2003 prints. R is 6,378,137 m. c is 299,792,458 m/s exactly. A day in the rates is 86,400 seconds. The GPS preset is the IS-GPS-200N radius 26,559,710 m, altitude 20,181.57 km, speed 3.874 km/s. It computes −7.21 μs/day from speed, +45.65 μs/day from gravity, and +38.44 μs/day net. NIST’s public page says 7, 45, and 38 microseconds per day. Ashby’s equation (35) prints 3 GM/(2 a c^2) + Φ0/c^2 = +2.5046×10^−10 − 6.9693×10^−10 = −4.4647×10^−10. That printed offset is +38.58 μs in 86,400 seconds. At the semi-major axis he prints, 2.656175×10^7 m, this page’s formulas still give −7.21, +45.65, and +38.44. The 0.14 μs/day gap is his geoid, L_G = 6.969290134×10^−10, against this page’s −GM/(R c^2). ISS at the 2023 lithograph’s about 420 km is −28.18, +3.71, net −24.47. Geostationary, from the fact-sheet 23.9345-hour sidereal day and this GM, is 35,786.07 km, net +46.45. The satellites desk’s 35,786.05 km uses the rounded fact-sheet GM. A test-particle circle at the Moon’s 384,400 km is speed 1.018 km/s and period 27.452 days. The fact sheet’s 1.022 km/s and 27.3217 days are not used. A slider runs to 0.99c, where one year aboard is 7.0888 years at home. Simplified weak-field model. Not for navigation.

entries.title: Solar-sail desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a solar-sail page. Irradiance is the IAU 2015 Resolution B3 nominal total solar irradiance, 1361 W/m², divided by the square of the distance in AU. c is 299,792,458 m/s exactly. A perfect absorber, face-on, feels 4.540 μN/m². A perfect reflector feels 9.080 μN/m², about 9.1 micronewtons on a square metre, because the light leaves with the opposite momentum. Kopp and Lean 2011 measured 1360.8 ± 0.5 W/m² at the 2008 minimum. That measurement is not substituted. The force on a flat sail is (S A cos θ / c) times (1−ρ) along the Sun line plus 2 ρ cos θ along the normal. Characteristic acceleration is the face-on value at 1 au. The lightness number is radiation acceleration over solar gravity, with the same resolution’s GM☉ of 1.3271244×10^20 m³/s². Both fall as 1/r², so the ratio does not change with distance. Lightness 1 would take 1.531 g/m². Δv = a × t holds the acceleration fixed and is labeled as that simplification. IKAROS is the JAXA side of 14 m, so 196 m², and the Tsuda et al. wet mass of 307 kg. The public page’s about 310 kg is not substituted. LightSail 2 is 32 m² and 4.93 kg from Mansell et al. 2023. The FCC filing’s 4.85 kg and the briefing’s 5 kg are not substituted. ACS3 is Wilkie’s 80 m² and 16 kg. His effective 0.045 mm/s² and lightness 0.0077, from a specular reflectance of 0.74, are not copied. This page’s perfect reflector for that area and mass is 0.0454 mm/s². Planet snaps are the fact-sheet J2000 semimajor axes. Not a trajectory.

entries.title: Fusion desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a fusion page. Energy is the mass defect times c². Atomic masses are AME2020. The conversion is the 2022 CODATA value, 931.49410372 MeV per u, and 1.66053906892×10^−27 kg per u. c and e are the exact SI defining constants. The pp net, 4 ¹H → ⁴He, is 0.02869687 u and 26.7310 MeV, which is 26.7 MeV to one digit after the decimal. The mass fraction is 0.712%, which is 0.7% to one digit. CNO has the same net masses because the catalysts return. D+T is 17.5893 MeV, the 17.6 MeV round. The two D+D branches are 3.2689 MeV and 4.0327 MeV. The triple-alpha net, 3 ⁴He → ¹²C, is 7.2747 MeV. Two ⁴He → ⁸Be is −0.0918 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon is recomputed from those masses. AME2020’s own column peaks at ⁶²Ni, 8794.5555 keV. ⁵⁸Fe is 8792.2534 keV. ⁵⁶Fe is 8790.3563 keV. The IAU 2015 nominal solar luminosity, 3.828×10^26 W, is 4.259×10^9 kg/s of mass. If the whole 26.7310 MeV leaves as that light, hydrogen is consumed at 5.983×10^11 kg/s. Neutrinos are named and not subtracted. Adelberger et al. 2011: the standard solar model is 99% pp and about 1% CN, and at solar-core temperature CNO scales about as T^18 against about T^4 for pp. NASA’s Sun facts put the core near 15 million °C. Not a stellar-evolution model.

entries.title: Light-time desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a light-time page. Pick a date and two bodies. The straight-line distance, in kilometres and astronomical units, is divided by c. One way is that quotient. The round trip is twice it. c is 299,792,458 m/s exactly, the SI defining constant. One astronomical unit is 149,597,870,700 m exactly, IAU 2012 Resolution B2, so 1 AU of light time is 499.005 seconds, 8.317 minutes, about 8.3 minutes. Planet places are JPL’s Approximate Positions of the Planets, Table 1, the Standish and Williams Keplerian elements valid 1800–2050. Earth is the Earth–Moon barycenter. The published heliocentric distance tolerances on that table include Mars at 25 × 1000 km and Jupiter at 600 × 1000 km. The Moon is a mean-distance circle at the Moon Fact Sheet semimajor axis, 384,400 km, period 27.3217 days. Perigee 363,300 km and apogee 405,500 km are labeled, not solved. The mean round trip is 2.564 seconds, about 2.5 seconds. Across 1800–2050 this model’s Earth–Mars one-way time runs from 3.100 to 22.257 light-minutes, roughly 3 to 22. A rover cannot be joysticked live. The card’s closest and farthest are one synodic period around the chosen date. Pluto keeps the historical row the solar map already uses, and the current JPL table publishes no Pluto tolerance. Voyager ranges are links to the JPL status page, not numbers stored here. Not a JPL Horizons ephemeris.

entries.title: Hydrogen spectra desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a hydrogen spectra page. The calculator is 1/λ = R_H (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with R_H = 1.09678×10^7 m⁻¹. That figure is the 2022 CODATA R_∞ = 10973731.568157 m⁻¹ times (m_p/m_e) / (m_p/m_e + 1), with m_p/m_e = 1836.152673426, which is 10967758.340 m⁻¹, rounded to six significant figures. h, c, and e are the exact SI defining constants on the same wallet, so a vacuum wavelength becomes a frequency and an energy in eV. With this constant, Lyman-alpha (2→1) is 121.568 nm, H-beta (4→2) is 486.272 nm, and H-alpha (3→2) is 656.467 nm. NIST ASD unresolved centers: Lyα observed and Ritz 121.56701 nm, vacuum, from the n = 2 center at 82259.158 cm⁻¹. Hα levels 82259.158 and 97492.304 cm⁻¹ differ by 15233.146 cm⁻¹, which is 656.463 nm in vacuum. ASD’s observed air wavelength is 656.279 nm and the Ritz air wavelength is 656.2819 nm. The customary unresolved air wavelength, the figure the redshift desk uses, is 656.280 nm. Hβ levels 82259.158 and 102823.904 cm⁻¹ give 486.269 nm in vacuum. The customary air wavelength is 486.132 nm. ASD’s observed air wavelength is 486.135 nm. The gaps are a few thousandths of a nanometre: the constant is rounded, and the Bohr jump is not one fine-structure component. The visible window is the NASA Imagine classroom cut, 400–700 nm. A redshift slider runs from z = 0 to z = 5. Lyman-alpha reaches 400 nm at z = 2.29034. Emission is bright lines on a dark field. Absorption is dark lines on a schematic continuum. The ladder is E_n = −hcR_H / n². Not a line list.

entries.title: Airmass desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an airmass page. Relative air mass is Kasten and Young 1989, m = [sin γ + 0.50572 (γ + 6.07995)^(−1.6364)]^(−1), with the apparent elevation in degrees. Their Table II lists 1.0000 at 90°, 1.9939 at 30°, 5.5841 at 10°, and 38.0868 at the horizon, and prints a relative error of +0.432% on that horizon row. This page evaluates the formula: 0.9997 at 90°, 1.9943 at 30°, 5.5860 at 10°, and 37.92 at 0°. Plane-parallel sec(z) is exactly 2 at 30° and has no finite value at 0°. Extinction in magnitudes is k times that air mass. Krisciunas et al. 1987 summit medians at 4200 m are B 0.19 and V 0.11. Krisciunas 1990, Table 2, a hazy night at Keaau, 75 m, on 19 December 1989, is V 0.341 ± 0.020. Bennett 1982 at apparent altitude 0°, 1010 hPa, and 10°C is 34.5′. NOAA’s sunrise altitude is −0.833°, about 34′ of refraction plus about 16′ of solar semi-diameter. The setting-Sun button puts the lower limb on the apparent horizon, and Bennett’s vertical diameter is shorter than 32′. Not a forecast.

entries.title: Impact scaling desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an asteroid and comet impact page. A sphere’s mass is m = π/6 · ρ · L³. Kinetic energy is E = ½mv², Collins, Melosh, and Marcus 2005 equation 1. One megaton on this page is 4.184 × 10^15 J. The paper prints 4.18 × 10^15 J. Equation 3 is the whole-Earth recurrence, about 109 × E^0.78 years. Equation 21 is the transient crater, constant 1.161 in rock and 1.365 in water, proportional to sin^(1/3) θ, with g_E = 9.81 m/s². Equation 22 multiplies by 1.25 when the transient crater is 2.56 km or smaller. Equation 27 is the complex rim, 1.17 × D_tc^1.13 / 3.2^0.13 km, above that. The two laws do not meet at the join. Water skips the collapse. A Barringer-like case, 42 m of iron at the program’s 8000 kg/m³, 15 km/s, 45°, and sedimentary rock, gives a final rim of 1.46 km. The Earth Impact Database rim is 1.186 km, inside the paper’s 0.8–1.5 constant band. Kring’s table of Collins et al. 2016 is 8.6 Mt at 3.2×10^8 kg. This density is lighter, so the megatons are recomputed. Chelyabinsk uses JPL’s about 18 m and 18.6 km/s. The same page also prints 17 m and nearly 500 kilotons, and Brown et al. 2013 print about 19 m (17–20 m) and 500 ± 100 kilotons. Tunguska uses 50 m, the low end of the NASA workshop abstract’s roughly 50–80 m, at the program’s 17 km/s, which is not a measured Tunguska speed. The abstract’s energy band is 10–20 megatons. Chicxulub’s 14 km is the program template. Morgan et al. 2022 describe an approximately 200 km structure and an energy of about 10^23 J. Entry is a qualitative note under 1 km. No airburst altitude. Not a hazard assessment.

entries.title: Meteor showers desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a meteor-shower page. The observed hourly rate is HR = ZHR × sin(h) / r^(6.5 − LM) × (1 − k). h is the radiant altitude in degrees. k is the obstructed fraction of the field. At or below the horizon the rate is 0. IMO’s major-shower table, ZHR 100 and limiting magnitude 6.5, prints 50 at 30°, 77 at 50°, and 17 at 10°. Those integers are the sine, rounded. A stated 50% cover is IMO’s field correction of 2, so that 50 becomes 25. The population index drops out at magnitude 6.5. One magnitude brighter, with r = 2, halves a zenith rate. Presets are IMO 2026 Table 5, dates for 2026: Quadrantids January 3, ZHR 80, 41 km/s, r 2.1, radiant 230° +49°, λ⊙ 283.15°; Lyrids April 22, ZHR 18, 49 km/s, r 2.1, 271° +34°, λ⊙ 32.32°, parent C/1861 G1 (Thatcher); Eta Aquariids May 6, ZHR 50, 66 km/s, r 2.4, 338° −1°, λ⊙ 45.5°; Perseids August 13, ZHR 100, 59 km/s, r 2.2, 48° +58°, λ⊙ 140.0°, parent 109P/Swift-Tuttle; Orionids October 21, ZHR 20, 66 km/s, r 2.5, 95° +16°, λ⊙ 208°; Leonids November 17, ZHR about 15, 71 km/s, r 2.5, 152° +22°, λ⊙ 235.27°, parent 55P/Tempel-Tuttle; Geminids December 14, ZHR 150, 35 km/s, r 2.6, 112° +33°, λ⊙ 262.2°. Parents the calendar text does not name are the JPL stream table: 196256 (2003 EH1), 1P/Halley, and 3200 Phaethon. Energy per gram is ½v². The Perseids’ 59 km/s is 1,740.5 kJ/g. Sky buttons: 6.5 is the IMO reference, 5.6 is the bright end of Bortle class 5, 4.5 is Bortle class 8 at best. Approximate. Not a forecast.

entries.title: Satellite orbits desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows an Earth-satellite page. Altitude runs from 160 km to 410,000 km. A circular orbit gives period, speed, orbits per mean solar day and per sidereal day, the westward ground-track step, the fraction of the surface in view, the horizon (line of sight and along the ground), and the nadir light-time round trip. Constants are the Earth Fact Sheet: GM 0.39860 × 10^6 km³/s², equatorial radius 6,378.137 km, sidereal rotation 23.9345 h, length of day 24.0000 h. c is 299,792.458 km/s. Geostationary, the circle whose period equals that sidereal day, is 35,786.05 km and 23 h 56.07 min at 3.075 km/s, and the ground track does not step. A 24-hour circle would sit 76.89 km higher. The Hohmann desk subtracts the volumetric radius from the same circle, a 7.137 km altitude difference. Presets use cited sizes and compute the rest: ISS about 420 km (NASA 2023 lithograph) is 92.97 min, 7.657 km/s, 15.489 orbits per solar day, 23.31° west; Hubble about 483 km (NASA Science) is 94.27 min; Starlink is the FCC-21-48A1 550 km shell; GPS is IS-GPS-200N AREF 26,559.710 km, altitude 20,181.57 km, 2.000 orbits per sidereal day; the Moon uses fact-sheet perigee 363,300 km and apogee 405,500 km. Earth’s GM alone does not reproduce the sheet’s 27.3217-day month. An ellipse is optional, with vis-viva at each end. Drag is named and not timed. Simplified two-body model. Circular unless an ellipse is set. Not for mission planning.

entries.title: Cosmology desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a cosmology page. A redshift becomes an age, a lookback time, and three distances, from a numerical integral of Hogg’s E(z) with no radiation term. Planck 2018 Table 2, column TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing: H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54, Ωm = 0.3153 ± 0.0073, ΩΛ = 0.6847 ± 0.0073. The published age for that column is 13.797 ± 0.023 Gyr, radiation included. This integral leaves radiation out and gives 13.801 Gyr. At z = 1: lookback 7.954 Gyr, age then 5.847 Gyr, comoving 3,402.7 Mpc (11.10 Gly), luminosity 6,805.4 Mpc (22.20 Gly), angular diameter 1,701.3 Mpc (5.55 Gly), 8.248 kpc per arcsec. Angular-diameter distance peaks at z = 1.588. SH0ES (Riess et al. 2022) H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 keeps the Planck densities, because that paper does not publish Ωm, and the age is 12.728 Gyr. Cited objects: Coma, Colless and Dunn 1996, mean cz = 6853 km/s so z = cz/c; 3C 273, SIMBAD z = 0.15756751; GN-z11, Bunker et al. 2023, z = 10.6034; CMB last scattering, Planck z* = 1089.92. The chart runs to z = 20, so the CMB marker is off the chart. r* = 144.43 Mpc is the sound horizon, not the distance to the CMB. Flat is the default. Curvature uses Hogg’s transverse distance. The redshift desk is the shift. The distance ladder stops at cz/H0. Not a fit and not a catalog.

entries.title: Distance ladder desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a distance-ladder page. The modulus is m − M = 5 log10(d / 10 pc) + A. A = 0 is the magnitude desk. m = 10, M = 0, A = 0 gives 1000 pc. A = 1 gives 10 × 10^1.8 pc, about 630.96 pc. The Sun at 10 pc stays at +4.83, and 10 pc is 32.616 ly. Parallax is d(pc) = 1/p(″). The fractional error σ_d/d equals σ_p/p, and the bounds 1/(p±σ) are asymmetric. Sirius is ESA’s worked example, p = 0.37921″, 1/p = 2.637 pc, with no uncertainty on that page. δ Cephei parallax is Benedict et al. 2007 Table 11: 3.66 ± 0.15 mas, so 1000/3.66 pc, near 1000/3.81 pc, far 1000/3.51 pc. Table 11’s (m−M)0 = 7.19 includes an LKH correction of −0.01 mag. Plain inversion is not that modulus, and this page does not apply LKH. The Cepheid line is the same paper, Table 12 column B07, Johnson V: M_V = −4.05 ± 0.02 + (−2.43 ± 0.12)(log10 P − 1). P = 10 d gives −4.05. δ Cephei Table 2 is P = 5.36627 d, ⟨V⟩ = 3.960, A_V = 0.23. The line gives M_V about −3.393. Table 11’s own M_V is −3.47 ± 0.11. The V residual scatter is 0.10 mag, a distance factor 10^0.02, shown as an illustration and not an error bar. Type Ia uses Richardson et al. 2014 Table 1, bias-corrected normal mean M_B = −19.25 ± 0.20, standard deviation 0.50 mag, N = 239. Hillebrandt and Niemeyer’s −19.30 is the H0 = 60 figure and is not the candle. SN 2011fe (Richmond and Smith 2012, Table 5): B max = 10.00 ± 0.02, A_B = 0.11 ± 0.03, so μ = 29.14 and the distance is about 6.730 Mpc. They adopt 29.10 ± 0.15 for M101, about 6.607 Mpc. The two are not forced to agree. Hubble flow is d = cz/H0. Coma (Colless and Dunn 1996) has mean cz = 6853 km/s and σ = 1082 km/s. Planck 67.4 gives about 101.68 Mpc. SH0ES 73.04 gives about 93.83 Mpc. The dispersion scale is larger than that gap. The bars are a sketch: Proxima’s 1.3 pc to 100 pc (NASA’s “a few hundred light-years”; NASA does not print 100 pc), Cepheids to ∼40 Mpc, Hubble flow ∼100–600 Mpc (Scolnic and Vincenzi). Not a catalog.

entries.title: Black hole desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a black-hole page for a non-rotating Schwarzschild hole. Mass runs from 1 to 10 billion solar masses on a log slider. r_s = 2GM/c². The photon sphere is 1.5 r_s. The ISCO is 3 r_s. The IAU 2015 nominal solar mass parameter, GM☉ = 1.3271244 × 10^20 m³ s^−2, and c = 299792458 m/s give r_s = 2.953 km. A hovering observer from 1.2 to 30 r_s reads √(1 − r_s/r). At 10 r_s that factor is 0.9487. The horizon tide across a 2 m body is 2GM L/r³, about 2.061×10^10 m/s² at one solar mass. Hawking temperature is ħ c³ / (8 π k GM), 6.170×10^−8 K at one solar mass. The evaporation time is the horizon-area estimate t = 5120 π G² M³ / (ħ c⁴), 2.095×10^67 Julian years at one solar mass, labeled an order of magnitude. Mean density uses the 2022 CODATA G, 6.67430 × 10^−11. Presets: 1 and 10 solar masses, computed; Cygnus X-1, 21.2 ± 2.2 M☉ (Miller-Jones et al. 2021); Sagittarius A*, (4.297 ± 0.012) × 10^6 M☉ statistical, systematics about 40,000 M☉ (GRAVITY Collaboration 2022, A&A 657, L12); M87*, 6.5 ± 0.2 (stat) ± 0.7 (sys) × 10^9 M☉ (EHT 2019, ApJL 875, L6). Real holes spin. Bardeen, Press, and Teukolsky 1972 move the photon orbit and the ISCO with that spin. This page holds them at 1.5 r_s and 3 r_s.

entries.title: Stellar lifetime desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a stellar-lifetime page. Mass runs from 0.1 to 60 solar masses on a log slider. Inside 0.179 < M ≤ 31, luminosity is the six-piece fit of Eker et al. 2018, Table 4: log10(L/L☉) = a log10(M/M☉) + b. The pieces are separate lines. They are not joined, and they are not used outside that window. At 1 M☉ the low-mass line gives log L = −0.007, about 0.984 L☉, not 1. Main-sequence lifetime is t ≈ 10 Gyr × M/L. With the IAU nominal L = 1 the Sun is exactly 10 Gyr. With the fit it is about 10.16 Gyr. The 10 Gyr zero is the classroom round number beside NASA’s 4.6-billion-year-old Sun plus about 5 billion years still on the main sequence (sum 9.6). It is not a model age. End-state labels follow NASA Science: under 8 M☉ a white dwarf, about 8 to 20 a neutron star, heavier a black hole. Heger et al. 2003 move those edges with metallicity, rotation, and mass loss. The plot marks the Planck 2018 age from Table 2, column TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing: 13.797 ± 0.023 Gyr. The +BAO column is 13.787 ± 0.020 Gyr. Cited presets: Proxima Centauri 0.120 ± 0.003 M☉ and 0.00151 ± 0.00008 L☉ (Ribas et al. 2017; below the fit; 10 × 0.120 / 0.00151 is about 795 Gyr), Sirius A 2.063 ± 0.023 M☉ and 24.74 ± 0.70 L☉ (Bond et al. 2017; about 834 Myr; YREC age 237 ± 15 Myr), Vega mass 2.15 M☉ with +0.10 and −0.15 (Monnier et al. 2012) and 44 ± 2 L☉ (Hill, Gulliver, and Adelman 2010; about 489 Myr, shorter than the cited 700 Myr age), Rigel log(L/L☉) = 5.08 and a track mass of 23 M☉ (Moravveji et al. 2012). Rigel is a blue supergiant, so the fit at 23 M☉ is not its present luminosity. Formula outputs are approximate scaling estimates. Not a stellar-evolution model.

entries.title: Telescope optics desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a telescope-optics page. Focal ratio is focal length over aperture. Magnification is telescope focal length over eyepiece focal length, and a Barlow multiplies that effective focal length. Exit pupil is aperture over magnification. The rough true field is apparent field divided by magnification. Light grasp compares the aperture with a 7 mm pupil, the traditional maximum Sky & Telescope states. Rayleigh’s criterion is 1.22 λ/D. Dawes’s empirical limit is printed as 116/D in millimetres and as 4.56/D in inches. A classroom 200 mm f/6 with a 25 mm eyepiece and a 50° apparent field is 48×, exit pupil 4.17 mm, true field 1.042° (62.5′), light grasp 816×, Rayleigh 0.692″ at 550 nm, and Dawes 0.580″ (116/D) and 0.579″ (4.56/D). At naked-eye magnitude 6.0 the collecting-area estimate is 13.28. Bowen’s 1947 formula gives 12.94. Hubble uses the STScI primer’s 2.4 m aperture at f/24, focal length 57.6 m. JWST uses NASA’s 6.5 m and 131.4 m, which compute to f/20.22. The 7×50, 80 mm, and 200 mm sets are round classroom numbers, not catalog models. Not a buying guide.

entries.title: Habitable zone desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a habitable-zone page: stellar flux S/S⊕ = (L/L☉)/d², and watts per square metre from the NASA Earth Fact Sheet solar irradiance, 1361.0 W/m². Equilibrium temperature assumes full heat redistribution and emissivity 1: T_eq = [F(1−A)/(4σ)]¼. Earth’s Bond albedo 0.294 at 1 AU gives S/S⊕ = 1.000 and T_eq = 255.1 K. The fact sheet’s average surface temperature is 288 K. The strip is Kopparapu et al. 2014, conservative and optimistic, 1 Earth mass, valid from 2600 K to 7200 K and not drawn outside that range. Presets: Venus, Earth, and Mars from the NASA fact sheets; Proxima Centauri b (Ribas et al. 2017; Anglada-Escudé et al. 2016); TRAPPIST-1 e (Agol et al. 2021), whose 2566 K host is below the polynomial; Kepler-452b (Jenkins et al. 2015). A point in the strip is not a habitability verdict.

entries.title: Transit and radial-velocity desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a transit page: depth δ ≈ (Rp/R*)², geometric probability about R*/a, a circular-orbit duration, and radial-velocity semi-amplitude K with m sin i. Masses are fact-sheet GM ratios, so G is not chosen. Earth–Sun, volumetric mean radii and i = 90°, is 83.86 ppm and 8.95 cm/s. Jupiter–Sun is 1.010% and 12.46 m/s. Cited presets: HD 209458 b (Bonomo et al. 2017), 51 Pegasi b (Cont et al. 2026; no planet radius, because the archive flags the composite radius as calculated), TRAPPIST-1 e (Agol et al. 2021), and GJ 1214 b (Mahajan, Eastman, and Kirk 2024). Uniform disk, no limb darkening, no eccentricity. Not a catalog and not a fitted light curve.

entries.title: HR diagram desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a Hertzsprung–Russell page: effective temperature across, hot on the left, and luminosity L/L☉ up. Radius lines are L = 4πR²σT⁴. σ is the CODATA value 5.670374419… × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. The zero is the IAU 2015 nominal Sun, 5772 K and 1 R☉, and the bolometric magnitude uses M_bol,☉ = 4.74. Cited central values: Proxima 2980 ± 80 K and 0.00151 ± 0.00008 L☉ (Ribas et al. 2017), Vega 9560 ± 30 K and 44 ± 2 L☉ (Hill, Gulliver, and Adelman 2010), Sirius A 9845 ± 64 K and 24.74 ± 0.70 L☉, Sirius B 25,369 ± 46 K and 0.02448 ± 0.00033 L☉ (Bond et al. 2017), Betelgeuse log(L/L☉) = 5.10 ± 0.22 (Dolan et al. 2016), Rigel log(L/L☉) = 5.08 (Moravveji et al. 2012). The Sun’s visual absolute magnitude +4.83 stays the fact-sheet figure, not the bolometric 4.74. Main sequence, giants, and white dwarfs are a classroom cartoon. Not a Gaia catalog and not an ephemeris.

entries.title: Redshift desk
entries.blurb: Astronomy grows a redshift page: z = (λ_obs − λ_rest)/λ_rest. At z = 1 the special-relativistic Doppler formula gives β = 0.6, while c·z equals the speed of light and is not a speed. Cosmological redshift is 1+z = a_now/a_then. The nearby Hubble toy is v = H0·d, with Planck 2018 H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc and SH0ES 2022 H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc. At a classroom 10 Mpc those central values are 674 km/s and 730.4 km/s. Cited presets: Andromeda z = −0.001 (SIMBAD), NGC 4258 z = 0.00158 (BASS DR2), 3C 273 z = 0.15756751 (SIMBAD), GN-z11 z = 10.6034 (Bunker et al. 2023).
